question.text: Ms. Anjali Krishnan, Head of Risk at Narmada Capital (Fund-of-AIFs), is reviewing the peer quartile rankings published by a commercial database. She notes that many wound-up / liquidated AIFs are NOT in the database, and some funds retroactively added their historical track record only after strong performance emerged. These two biases are called, respectively:

answer.text: Survivorship bias and backfill (self-selection / incubation) bias.

explanation.text: The Logic: Survivorship bias: dead/wound-up funds drop out of the database, inflating average returns of survivors. Backfill (a.k.a. self-selection / incubation) bias: funds only add themselves AFTER strong track record, skewing early-year returns upward. Both are standard hedge-fund and PE database pitfalls that a Cat I FoF manager must adjust for when selecting GPs. The Trap: Option A names real biases (vintage-mismatch, currency) but they describe different problems. Option B invents 'credit-rating bias' and uses 'liquidity' loosely. Option D names biases from behavioural finance (home-country, recency) that are investor-level, not database-level. Cross-Exam Context: XV (Research Analyst) covers survivorship bias in equity fund research. XIX-C extends it to AIF peer-benchmark databases (Preqin, PitchBook, CRISIL). Manager's Pro-Tip: When citing peer quartile to LPs, always caveat 'based on Preqin 2019-vintage India Cat I sample, which may be subject to survivorship/backfill bias.' This pre-empts sophisticated LP pushback and protects you from misrepresentation claims under SEBI AIF Reg 10(c).
